items.title: Overview
items.text: This document provides detailed documentation for all implemented sources, stages, and sinks in TRAM.

items.title: Available Sources
items.text: Name Type Description broker broker Receives OTLP data from a message broker through a driver (NATS JetStream, Kafka, AMQP 1.0) buffer buffer Reads a queue on the instance's disk that a Buffer Sink writes, through a driver (SQLite), and delivers it with retries; see Buffers generator generator Emits empty events at a fixed interval, for testing pipelines otlp otlp Receives protobuf-encoded OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) data via HTTP

items.title: Available Stages
items.text: Name Type Description batch batch Merges concurrently arriving events into larger batches decryption decryption Decrypts log record bodies and selected attributes encrypted by the encryption stage delay delay Holds every event back for a fixed duration encryption encryption Encrypts log record bodies and selected attributes before the sinks filter filter Keeps only the records that match the rules of its driver, e.g. CEL noop noop Pass-through stage that does no processing (useful for testing) validation validation Accepts, drops or rejects whole events by the rules of its driver, e.g. CEL value_map value_map Copies an attribute value to another attribute by looking it up in a table

items.title: Available Sinks
items.text: Name Type Description broker broker Sends OTLP data to a message broker through a driver (NATS JetStream, Kafka, AMQP 1.0), with the destination of each record computed by CEL buffer buffer Stores OTLP data durably in a queue on the instance's disk through a driver (SQLite), for a Buffer Source to deliver; see Buffers debug debug Writes events to the log (stderr) for debugging and development otlp otlp Sends OTLP-encoded events via HTTP to an OpenTelemetry endpoint

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Component Type vs Name: The type field in configuration refers to the component implementation type (e.g., generator, validation), while the name field is a user-defined identifier for the component instance within a stream.
  • Connections: The from field in stages and sinks specifies which component they receive data from.
  • Tree Structure: Pipelines form a tree with the source as root, stages as intermediate nodes, and sinks as leaves.
  • Delivery Guarantee: Delivery is at-least-once, and TRAM does not deduplicate. A sink can receive the same data again, e.g. when a client retries after a 503 although some sinks had already accepted the data, when a broker message is redelivered after one branch of its stream failed, or when a publish succeeded but its acknowledgement was lost. Deduplicate at the destination where duplicates matter.

items.title: Buffers
items.text:
A buffer rides out outages of a destination by storing events on the instance's disk: one stream writes them with a Buffer Sink, another reads them with a Buffer Source and delivers them. The queue name connects the two. Pipelines stay synchronous and in memory; the queue is a broker embedded in the instance, and the Buffer Source handles deliveries like the Broker Source.

stream otlp-to-buffer:  OTLP Source ──▶ Buffer Sink   (queue: outbox)
stream buffer-to-otlp:  Buffer Source (queue: outbox) ──▶ batch ──▶ OTLP Sink
  • The queue is local. A Buffer Source reads only the queue of its own instance. Run both streams on the same instance, on Kubernetes on the same Engine; every instance then has a queue of its own
  • Data directory. Queues live in tram server --data-dir, which has to be on a volume that outlives the process. Without it, streams with a buffer sink or source fail to build. On Kubernetes, an Engine with storage gives every instance a volume and sets it
  • One process per queue. A queue file is locked by the instance that uses it; another process cannot open it
  • Retention. The writing sink sets max_age, which the queue keeps. Deleting or suspending the reading stream discards nothing: the events wait until a reader comes back or they expire, like messages of a broker without a consumer
  • Draining a buffer. Suspend the writing stream and keep the reading one running until the queue is empty. On Kubernetes, the volumes of instances that go are drained by Jobs through the reading streams, also suspended ones; to remove an Engine's storage, suspend the writing streams first, see Removing storage
  • Throughput. Every commit is synced to disk, so the latency of the volume limits the throughput. Size the volume above max_bytes, which counts the payloads only, for the write-ahead log and space not yet returned to the file system

items.title: Suspended Streams
items.text: A stream with "suspended": true stays defined but does not run: its source is not started, and its stages and sinks are not built, so it opens no port and reads from no broker or buffer. Setting it back to false starts the stream again. Use it to pause a stream, e.g. during maintenance of a destination, or to drain a buffer.

items.title: Hold Times
items.text:
A source like OTLP waits for a delivery only for a limited time, its delivery_timeout, and then answers with 503. batch stages can hold an event back for up to their timeout, delay stages for their delay. When a stream is created or updated, TRAM adds up these hold times on the way from the source to each sink and rejects the stream if the sum reaches the source's limit: every event that does not fill its batch would be cancelled, so the stream would fail as soon as traffic gets low. The error names the stages:

stream spec is invalid: on the way to sink openobserve-traces, batch-traces (10s) can hold an event for 10s, but source otlp cancels deliveries after 8s

An update that is rejected leaves the running stream unchanged. Shorten the timeout or delay, or raise the source's delivery_timeout, and keep that below the time the clients wait. Sources without such a limit, like the Broker Source, are not checked.

items.title: Sinks
items.text: Sinks are the terminal points of a pipeline that consume or export data.

items.title: Debug Sink
items.text:
Writes every event to the log on stderr as a Debug event record with the attributes path (the path through the stream, e.g. in -> filter -> out), records (number of log records, data points and spans) and event (the full OTLP data). For development, testing and debugging.

Type: debug

Configuration: None required.

Example:

{
  "name": "console-output",
  "type": "debug",
  "from": "source"
}

items.title: OTLP Sink
items.text:
Sends OpenTelemetry Protocol data via HTTP to an OTLP-compatible endpoint. Sends logs to /v1/logs, metrics to /v1/metrics, and traces to /v1/traces with a protobuf-encoded body.

Type: otlp

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description url string Without url_expression - OTLP HTTP endpoint URL (e.g., "http://localhost:4318") url_expression object No - Sends each entry to the URL a CEL expression returns, see Routing by URL headers object No - HTTP headers to send with each request timeout string No "10s" HTTP request timeout as a Go duration (e.g., "5s", "30s") insecure boolean No false Allow connections to servers with invalid TLS certificates

Example:

{
  "name": "otlp-sink",
  "type": "otlp",
  "from": "source",
  "spec": {
    "url": "http://telemetry-collector:4318"
  }
}

Example with authentication and custom timeout:

{
  "name": "secure-otlp-sink",
  "type": "otlp",
  "from": "filter-stage",
  "spec": {
    "url": "https://telemetry-collector:4318",
    "timeout": "30s",
    "headers": {
      "Authorization": "Bearer your-api-key-here"
    }
  }
}

Example with invalid certificate acceptance (for testing):

{
  "name": "dev-otlp-sink",
  "type": "otlp",
  "from": "source",
  "spec": {
    "url": "https://localhost:4318",
    "insecure": true
  }
}
Behavior
  • Each signal type of an event is sent as a separate HTTP request to its endpoint. An event can hold several signal types, e.g. after a batch stage; if one request fails, the source retries the whole event, so the others may be sent twice
  • Uses protobuf encoding (application/x-protobuf content type) as required by OTLP/HTTP
  • The sink handles URL construction properly, so both "http://host:4318" and "http://host:4318/" work correctly
  • Non-2xx answers fail the delivery. Client errors that refuse the data itself (4xx except 408 and 429) reject the event, so the OTLP source answers with 422 and the Broker Source rejects the message. Other errors, including 408, 429 and 5xx, can be retried by the source: the OTLP source answers with 503, the Broker Source has the message redelivered
  • Proxy settings are taken from the HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY environment variables
  • Connection pooling is used for better performance with multiple requests
  • Timeout applies to the entire request lifecycle, including connection establishment and reading the response
  • The requests of an event are sent at the same time, at most 16 at once. If one fails in a way that may go away, e.g. with 503, the event fails retriably even if another destination rejected its data, so the source retries all of it. Only if every failed request was rejected is the event rejected

items.title: Routing by URL
items.text:
With url_expression, the sink sends each log record, metric data point and span to the URL its expression returns, e.g. to a tenant's own endpoint. It groups the entries by URL and sends one request per URL and signal type.

Field Type Required Default Description logs string One of logs, metrics, traces - CEL expression returning the URL of a log record metrics string One of logs, metrics, traces - CEL expression returning the URL of a metric data point traces string One of logs, metrics, traces - CEL expression returning the URL of a span
  • The expressions have the same variables and get_attr function as the destination expressions of the Broker Sink, e.g. record, resource and datapoint. Metrics are split per data point the same way
  • A URL is the base URL like url; the sink appends /v1/logs, /v1/metrics or /v1/traces. It must be http or https and have a host. An expression that fails, does not return a string, or returns another URL rejects the event. get_attr returns "" for a missing attribute, which is not a valid URL
  • Signals without an expression are sent to url. Without url, they are not sent
  • headers, timeout and insecure apply to every destination
  • The data decides where it is sent. Make sure only trusted values can reach the expression, e.g. by deriving the URL from a tenant ID that a validation stage checks, rather than taking a URL from an attribute

Example with an endpoint per tenant:

{
  "name": "tenant-otlp",
  "type": "otlp",
  "from": "validator",
  "spec": {
    "url_expression": {
      "logs": "'https://' + record.attributes.get_attr('tenant.id') + '.otlp.example.com'"
    }
  }
}

items.title: Broker Sink
items.text:
Sends OTLP data to a message broker chosen by driver (driver options under nats:, kafka:, amqp:). A CEL expression per signal computes each record's destination; the records of one signal and destination become one message. The broker is set up outside TRAM: the sink creates no streams, topics or queues.

Type: broker

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description driver string Yes - The broker: nats (NATS JetStream), kafka (Apache Kafka and compatible brokers) or amqp (AMQP 1.0) destination object Yes - CEL expressions per signal (logs, metrics, traces, at least one) that return the destination of each record, e.g. the NATS subject. Signals without an expression are not sent max_pending int No 256 How many messages the sink sends before it waits for their acknowledgements. The broker has to store them as they arrive partition object No - Spreads records over partitions, see Partitioning nats object With driver: nats - Options of the NATS driver: url (required) kafka object With driver: kafka - Options of the Kafka driver: brokers (required), tls and sasl as for the Broker Source, and max_message_bytes (default 1 MiB), the largest message sent; keep it at or below the broker's message.max.bytes amqp object With driver: amqp - Options of the AMQP driver: url (required), username, password and insecure_skip_verify as for the Broker Source (which also covers Solace), and max_message_bytes, the largest message sent (default: only the limit the broker announces per address)

CEL Expression Context:

Expression Variables logs logs (payload), resource (Resource), scope (InstrumentationScope), record (LogRecord) metrics metrics (payload), resource, scope, metric (Metric), datapoint (the data point; its type depends on the metric type) traces traces (payload), resource, scope, span (Span)

With partitioning, the expressions also have partition (int), the partition of the record, data point or span.

  • Each expression is evaluated once per log record, metric data point and span and must return a string. The payload variable holds only the current log record, metric or span with its resource and scope, so [0] indexes address it, e.g. logs.resource_logs[0].scope_logs[0].log_records[0]. For metrics it holds the whole metric with all its data points
  • resource and scope are empty messages when the payload has none. Field names follow the OTLP protobuf definitions, e.g. record.severity_text, datapoint.attributes
  • Metrics are routed per data point: a metric whose data points resolve to different destinations is split into one metric per destination, each with the metric's name, description, unit, metadata and type-specific fields. A metric whose data points all resolve to the same destination is sent as it is
  • A metric without data points is evaluated once without datapoint; an expression that reads it fails for that metric and rejects the event
  • The custom function get_attr(key) on an attribute list returns the string value of an attribute, or "" if it is missing, e.g. resource.attributes.get_attr('service.name')

Example:

{
  "name": "to-routers",
  "type": "broker",
  "from": "map-router",
  "spec": {
    "driver": "nats",
    "nats": { "url": "nats://localhost:4222" },
    "destination": {
      "logs": "'router.audit.' + record.attributes.get_attr('example.router.id') + '.logs'"
    },
    "max_pending": 256
  }
}
Behavior
  • One signal per destination. Messages name no signal, so a consumer can only decode a destination that holds one signal. Give each signal its own destinations, e.g. by a signal token in the subject
  • Records keep their resource and scope. If all records of a signal resolve to the same destination, the payload is sent unchanged. Resources that appear in several entries of an event, e.g. after a batch stage, stay separate entries in the message, which OTLP allows
  • An event is rejected if a destination expression fails for one of its records, does not return a string, or returns a destination the driver refuses, e.g. a NATS subject with an empty token, whitespace or a wildcard. get_attr returns "" for a missing attribute, so 'logs.' + ...get_attr('team') gives the invalid logs. for records without it. The OTLP source answers with HTTP 422, the Broker Source rejects the message instead of redelivering it
  • A message larger than the broker accepts (NATS: the server's max_payload) rejects the event instead of failing on every retry. Messages of the event sent before it stay sent. Keep batches small enough that the largest message per destination stays below the limit
  • The sink encodes and sends the messages of an event one after another without waiting in between, and reports success once the broker has acknowledged every message. If one cannot be sent or is not acknowledged within 10 seconds, the event fails and the source retries it, so messages already stored are stored again
  • NATS: JetStream stores each message in the stream whose subjects cover its subject; a subject no stream covers fails the publish (503 at the OTLP source). Set the streams up before the sink sends, e.g. with NACK or the nats CLI
  • NATS: each sink has its own connection. A lost connection is retried every 2 seconds, with up to 1 second of jitter, for as long as the sink runs. While disconnected, publishing fails at once instead of being buffered, so the OTLP source answers with 503 and clients retry until NATS is back
  • Kafka: destinations are topics, which may contain letters, digits, ., _ and -, at most 249 characters. A topic that does not exist fails the send after a few metadata retries (503 at the OTLP source); TRAM creates no topics. Messages have no key, so Kafka spreads them over the topic's partitions; with partitioning, put the partition into the topic name
  • Kafka: max_pending bounds the records buffered and in flight; a record not acknowledged within 10 seconds, retries included, fails the event
  • AMQP: destinations are addresses, in the broker's form; the sink refuses only empty addresses and whitespace and leaves the rest to the broker. Each address gets its own sender link on one connection. Up to max_pending messages are sent at once, each waiting for the broker's disposition for up to 10 seconds. A lost connection is opened again on the next message, so the OTLP source answers 503 until the broker is back

items.title: Broker Partitioning
items.text:
With partition, the sink computes a partition per record from a key, e.g. the tenant, and gives it to the destination expressions as partition. Put it into the destination, e.g. 'audit.' + string(partition) + '.' + ..., and set up one stream per partition, so each stream holds a part of the data and the streams can be led by different servers.

Field Type Required Default Description count int Yes - Number of partitions, from 1 to 1024 logs string With destination.logs - CEL expression returning the key of a log record. Has the same variables as the destination expression, without partition metrics string With destination.metrics - CEL expression returning the key of a metric data point traces string With destination.traces - CEL expression returning the key of a span
  • The partition of a key is its 32-bit FNV-1a hash modulo count, the same as the former NATS sink's. It never changes, so consumers can compute which partition holds a key; the Broker Source does so with its partition field
  • An expression for the key that fails or does not return a string rejects the event. A missing attribute gives the key "", which is a valid key like any other
  • Changing count moves keys to other partitions. Data already stored stays where it is, so changing it is a migration

items.title: Buffer Sink
items.text:
Stores every event durably in a queue on the instance's disk, from which a Buffer Source of the same instance delivers it. The sink returns once the event is synced to disk, so an OTLP client gets 200, and a Broker Source acknowledges its message, when the event is stored, not when it is delivered; see Buffers.

Type: buffer

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description driver string Yes - The storage of the queue: sqlite sqlite object With driver: sqlite - Options of the SQLite driver; it has none yet, so {} queue string Yes - The queue to write: letters, digits and . _ -, starting with a letter or digit. SQLite keeps it in <data dir>/<queue>.db max_age string No "24h" How long an event waits for its delivery at most, as a Go duration. It is kept with the queue, so its readers and drains know it max_bytes int No 1073741824 (1 GiB) Size of the stored payloads at which the sink refuses further events with an error sources retry (503 for OTLP clients) max_pending int No 256 Events handed to the queue but not yet synced; the sink waits beyond it

Example:

{
  "name": "outbox",
  "type": "buffer",
  "from": "otlp-in",
  "spec": {
    "driver": "sqlite",
    "sqlite": {},
    "queue": "outbox",
    "max_age": "24h",
    "max_bytes": 10737418240
  }
}
Behavior
  • An event is stored as one entry per signal. Concurrent events are stored in one commit, which is synced to disk before their callers return; there is no added delay
  • An event larger than max_bytes by itself is rejected (422 for OTLP clients), since it can never fit
  • Without a data directory (tram server --data-dir), the stream fails to build
  • Metrics of the queue are not recorded yet; a queue that holds events but has no Buffer Source in the instance is logged every 10 minutes

items.title: Sources
items.text: Sources are the entry points of a pipeline that produce or receive data events.

items.title: Generator Source
items.text:
Emits an empty event at a fixed interval, for testing how a stream is wired. Stages that count or inspect records, like batch or filter, ignore the events.

Type: generator

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description interval string Yes - Time interval between events (e.g., "5s", "1m")

Example:

{
  "name": "event-generator",
  "type": "generator",
  "spec": {
    "interval": "5s"
  }
}

items.title: OTLP Source
items.text:
Receives OpenTelemetry Protocol data over HTTP (OTLP/HTTP). OTLP over gRPC is not supported.

Type: otlp

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description http_port int Yes - Port to listen on, on all network interfaces delivery_timeout string No "8s" Maximum time to pass a request on to the stages and sinks, as a Go duration. A request that takes longer is cancelled and answered with 503, which clients retry retry_after string No "5s" How long clients should wait before retrying a 503, as a Go duration. Sent as the Retry-After header in whole seconds, rounded up

Example:

{
  "name": "otlp-receiver",
  "type": "otlp",
  "spec": {
    "http_port": 4318
  }
}

Responses:

Status When 200 Empty response message in the request's encoding, once all sinks have accepted the data 422 Body cannot be read or parsed, contains a duplicate key, or holds data rejected by a stage or sink (e.g. validation with on_mismatch: reject) 413 Body larger than 20 MiB, also after decompression 415 Other content types or encodings 503 Passing the data on failed or took longer than delivery_timeout; sent with a Retry-After header. The only status OTLP clients retry — the only answer the request itself did not cause Behavior
  • Accepts POST requests on /v1/logs, /v1/metrics and /v1/traces with a protobuf (application/x-protobuf) or JSON (application/json) body. Requests without a content type are read as protobuf
  • Bodies may be compressed with Content-Encoding: gzip
  • Each request becomes one event and is passed on as a whole
  • A request in which a key appears twice in the same key-value list is refused with 422: the attributes of a resource, scope, log record, span, span event, span link, data point or exemplar, a metric's metadata, and key-value lists nested in values or log bodies. OTLP requires unique keys; with a key twice, a stage could check one value while a sink routes by the other. The same key in different lists, e.g. on the resource and on a record, is allowed
  • A rejection is answered with 422 wherever it comes from, including a sink whose destination refuses the data permanently, e.g. an OTLP Sink whose destination answers 401, 403 or 404 because of its own configuration. The client then drops data it did not cause to be refused
  • The default delivery_timeout is below the 10s that OpenTelemetry SDK exporters wait by default, so they get the 503 before they give up. batch and delay stages have to leave time for it, see Hold Times. Raise it for pipelines that take longer, e.g. with a delay stage or slow sinks, and for clients that wait longer, like the OpenTelemetry Collector (30s by default). A batch that is already being sent when the timeout expires is still awaited, since it holds data of other requests too
  • A request may take up to 1 minute to send, which leaves time for large bodies on slow connections
  • The port is opened when the stream is created, so a port that is already in use fails the stream creation

items.title: Broker Source
items.text:
Receives OTLP data from a message broker chosen by driver (driver options under nats:, kafka:, amqp:). Every message is one serialized OTLP LogsData, MetricsData or TracesData — the plain body the Broker Sink writes, so any producer can feed the source. The broker is set up outside TRAM; the source creates or updates only its consumer.

Type: broker

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description driver string Yes - The broker: nats (NATS JetStream), kafka (Apache Kafka and compatible brokers) or amqp (AMQP 1.0, e.g. ActiveMQ Artemis, RabbitMQ 4, Solace, Azure Service Bus) signal string Yes - What every message holds: logs, metrics or traces. Messages name no signal themselves, so a source reads one signal; read several with one source each workers int No 1 Number of messages processed concurrently (1-10000) partition object No - Reads the partition of a key from data a Broker Sink spread over partitions: count (1-1024) as in the sink, and the required key. {partition} in the driver's options is replaced by the key's partition nats object With driver: nats - Options of the NATS driver, see below kafka object With driver: kafka - Options of the Kafka driver, see below amqp object With driver: amqp - Options of the AMQP driver, see below

NATS driver options (nats):

Field Type Required Default Description url string Yes - NATS server URL, e.g. nats://localhost:4222 subject string Yes - Subject filter of the consumer; wildcards like logs.* are allowed stream string No - Stream that holds subject. Without it, the stream is looked up by subject when the source starts durable string No - Name of a durable consumer. Without it, a temporary consumer is created whenever the source is created

Kafka driver options (kafka):

Field Type Required Default Description brokers array[string] Yes - Seed brokers, host:port topic string Yes - Topic to read, from all its partitions group string Yes - Consumer group. Sources that share it split the partitions; the group's committed offsets are where a source continues tls object No - Connect with TLS and the system's certificate authorities; insecure_skip_verify: true skips the verification, for tests only sasl object No - Authenticate: mechanism (plain, scram-sha-256 or scram-sha-512), username, password. In a Stream resource, take them from a secret with valueFrom.secretKeyRef

AMQP 1.0 driver options (amqp):

Field Type Required Default Description url string Yes - Broker URL, amqp://host:5672 or amqps://host:5671 address string Yes - Address to read, e.g. a queue. Its form depends on the broker: a queue name on ActiveMQ Artemis and Solace, /queues/<name> on RabbitMQ 4 username, password string No - Authenticate with SASL PLAIN; without them the connection uses SASL ANONYMOUS. In a Stream resource, take them from a secret with valueFrom.secretKeyRef insecure_skip_verify bool No false Skip the verification of the broker's certificate with amqps, for tests only Solace with the AMQP driver

Solace PubSub+ brokers speak AMQP 1.0, so they are used through driver: amqp; TRAM has no Solace driver of its own, because Solace's Go API needs cgo and TRAM's image is a static binary.

  • Enable the AMQP service of the message VPN. Solace gives each message VPN its own AMQP port, plain text and TLS (amqps://); use that port in url
  • username and password are a client username of the message VPN; it needs permission to publish to the destinations of a sink and to consume from the queue of a source
  • A source's address is the name of a queue, set up outside TRAM with consume permission for the client username. A retried message is returned as a failed delivery, so the queue's maximum redelivery count and its dead message queue apply. A sink's destinations are queue names, or topics in Solace's AMQP address syntax
  • This combination is not covered by TRAM's automated tests: the Solace container needs a user ID that rootless Podman with the default subordinate ID range cannot map. The AMQP driver is tested against ActiveMQ Artemis; verify against your Solace version before relying on it

Example:

{
  "name": "audit-in",
  "type": "broker",
  "spec": {
    "driver": "nats",
    "signal": "logs",
    "workers": 64,
    "nats": {
      "url": "nats://localhost:4222",
      "subject": "audit.logs",
      "durable": "audit"
    }
  }
}
Behavior
  • A message that is not valid OTLP data of signal is rejected and not redelivered. Protobuf does not name its type, so data of another signal may decode without error; keep one signal per subject
  • Each message becomes one event. A message is acknowledged once all sinks have accepted it. If passing it on fails, it is redelivered after 5 seconds; data rejected by a stage or sink is rejected for good
  • Delivery is at-least-once, and messages are not processed in order unless workers is 1
  • Up to workers messages are processed at the same time. The driver buffers only as many messages as there are workers, so no message waits long for a worker while its acknowledgement deadline runs
  • A batch stage after the source holds up to workers messages, since every message waits for its batch to be delivered before it is acknowledged. To let batches fill up to max_records before their timeout, set workers to at least max_records divided by the records per message
  • Stopping or updating the source interrupts waiting for new messages right away; messages being processed are still delivered and acknowledged
  • With partition, the source computes the partition of key like the Broker Sink and replaces {partition} in every option of the driver. Without partition, the options must not contain it; with it, at least one must
  • NATS: the consumer starts at the beginning of the stream. A durable consumer continues where it stopped. Its MaxAckPending is twice workers, at least 1,000, the JetStream default; the limit applies across all TRAM replicas that share a durable consumer
  • NATS: with large messages and many workers, NATS can have a lot of data to send to the source at once. If that exceeds what the server buffers for one connection (max_pending, 64 MB by default), the server disconnects the source as a slow consumer, and the messages it had sent come again after their acknowledgement deadline. Lower workers, or raise max_pending above workers × message size
  • NATS: a lost connection is retried every 2 seconds, with up to 1 second of jitter, for as long as the source runs. A stream that does not exist when the source starts fails the TRAM stream, which is retried
  • Kafka: offsets are committed per partition, every second and when the source stops, and only up to the first message that is not done yet, so messages finished out of order are never skipped by a restart. A message that is retried comes again after the delay from the same source; its offset stays uncommitted until it is done, so a restart reads it again. A rejected message counts as done; TRAM writes no dead-letter topic
  • Kafka: a topic that does not exist when the source starts fails the TRAM stream, which is retried. A group rebalance hands partitions to other sources; messages of those partitions that were not done yet are read again by their new owner
  • AMQP: the source has credit for twice workers messages. AMQP 1.0 has no delayed redelivery: a retried message is held for the delay and then returned as a failed delivery, which counts towards the broker's limit of attempts before it dead-letters the message; it keeps its credit while held. A rejected message is settled as rejected, and the broker's policy decides what happens to it, usually a dead-letter address
  • AMQP: a lost connection is opened again with growing delays, up to 5 seconds; messages not settled on the lost connection are delivered again by the broker. An address the broker does not have fails the TRAM stream when it starts, unless the broker creates addresses on demand

items.title: Buffer Source
items.text:
Reads the queue a Buffer Sink of the same instance writes and delivers its events to the stages and sinks of its stream. A delivery that fails is retried with exponential backoff until the queue's max_age; see Buffers for how the two streams work together.

Type: buffer

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description driver string Yes - The storage of the queue: sqlite sqlite object With driver: sqlite - Options of the SQLite driver; it has none yet, so {} queue string Yes - The queue to read: letters, digits and . _ -, starting with a letter or digit. The same name as in the Buffer Sink workers int No 1 Number of events delivered at once (1-10000) retry_initial string No "1s" Delay before the first retry of a failed delivery, as a Go duration; it doubles with every failure retry_max string No "5m" Longest delay between retries signal string No - Only for drivers whose queues do not record the signal; SQLite does, so a source reads logs, metrics and traces alike

Example:

{
  "name": "outbox",
  "type": "buffer",
  "spec": {
    "driver": "sqlite",
    "sqlite": {},
    "queue": "outbox",
    "workers": 4,
    "retry_initial": "1s",
    "retry_max": "5m"
  }
}
Behavior
  • An event that a node below rejects for good, e.g. a 422 of the destination, is removed at once; an event older than the queue's max_age is removed after its next failed delivery, or by the cleanup every minute. Both are logged as warnings
  • Delivery is at-least-once: an event is delivered again if the instance stops during its delivery. The order of deliveries is not guaranteed
  • Retries keep their schedule across restarts. An event whose delivery was interrupted by a restart is delivered again right away
  • Like the Broker Source, it waits for nothing: its stages and sinks get each event as soon as it is due, and their hold times do not count against any timeout of the source
  • Without a data directory (tram server --data-dir), the stream fails to build

items.title: Stages
items.text: Stages process, transform, or filter data between sources and sinks.

items.title: Filter Stage
items.text:
Keeps only the records that match the rules of the driver chosen by driver, decided per log record, metric data point and span. The driver's options are under the driver's name, e.g. cel:. To accept or reject whole events instead, use the Validation Stage.

Type: filter

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description driver string Yes - The technology of the rules: cel (Common Expression Language) cel object With driver: cel - Options of the CEL driver, see below

CEL driver options:

Field Type Required Default Description logs string One of logs, metrics, traces - CEL expression evaluated per log record. Must return a boolean metrics string One of logs, metrics, traces - CEL expression evaluated per metric data point. Must return a boolean traces string One of logs, metrics, traces - CEL expression evaluated per span. Must return a boolean

Signal types without an expression are passed on unfiltered. Use "false" to remove a signal type completely.

CEL Expression Context:

Expression Variables logs resource (Resource), scope (InstrumentationScope), record (LogRecord) metrics resource, scope, metric (Metric), datapoint (the data point; its type depends on the metric type) traces resource, scope, span (Span)

resource and scope are empty messages when the payload has none, so their fields can be accessed without checks. Field names follow the OTLP protobuf definitions, e.g. record.severity_text, span.name, datapoint.attributes.

Example: split logs by customer into two branches:

"stages": [
  {
    "name": "customer-a",
    "type": "filter",
    "from": "otlp-in",
    "spec": {
      "driver": "cel",
      "cel": {
        "logs": "record.attributes.exists(a, a.key == 'customer' && a.value.string_value == 'A')"
      }
    }
  },
  {
    "name": "other-customers",
    "type": "filter",
    "from": "otlp-in",
    "spec": {
      "driver": "cel",
      "cel": {
        "logs": "!record.attributes.exists(a, a.key == 'customer' && a.value.string_value == 'A')"
      }
    }
  }
]

Additional Examples (the cel options):

Keep only ERROR logs: 

{ "logs": "record.severity_text == 'ERROR'" }

Keep only the data points of one metric: 

{ "metrics": "metric.name == 'http.server.request.duration'" }

Keep only spans of one service: 

{ "traces": "resource.attributes.exists(a, a.key == 'service.name' && a.value.string_value == 'checkout')" }

Behavior
  • Kept records are passed on in their original resource and scope; nothing is copied, and containers without remaining records are removed. If no record is kept, nothing is passed on
  • When splitting into branches, write the last branch as the negation of the others, so every record ends up in exactly one branch
  • A rule that fails for a record, e.g. a CEL expression accessing a missing list index, rejects the whole event. The OTLP source answers with HTTP 422, the Broker Source rejects the message instead of redelivering it
  • Place a batch stage before the filters to merge many small requests first; each branch then receives one filtered batch

items.title: Validation Stage
items.text:
Checks each incoming event as a whole — one OTLP request, one broker message, or one batch — against the rules of the driver chosen by driver, and passes it on, drops it, or rejects it. The driver's options are under the driver's name, e.g. cel:. To keep only matching records, use the Filter Stage.

Type: validation

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description driver string Yes - The technology of the rules: cel (Common Expression Language) on_mismatch string Yes - Action when a signal does not match its rule: "drop" or "reject" cel object With driver: cel - Options of the CEL driver, see below

CEL driver options:

Field Type Required Default Description logs string No - CEL expression evaluated once for all logs of an event. Must return a boolean. Without it, all logs match metrics string No - CEL expression evaluated once for all metrics of an event. Must return a boolean. Without it, all metrics match traces string No - CEL expression evaluated once for all traces of an event. Must return a boolean. Without it, all traces match

CEL Expression Context: - Each expression receives the complete payload of its signal type: logs (LogsData), metrics (MetricsData), or traces (TracesData) - An event can contain several signal types, e.g. after a batch stage. Each type present is checked with its own expression - Use the full protobuf structure, e.g. logs.resource_logs.all(...), and write the expression as a condition that every accepted delivery has to fulfil

On Mismatch Behavior: - drop - Removes all data of the signal type that did not match. Other signal types of the event are still passed on; if nothing is left, nothing is passed on - reject - Rejects the whole event with an error. The OTLP source answers with HTTP 422, the Broker Source rejects the message instead of redelivering it

Example: reject log deliveries in which a resource has no service.name:

{
  "name": "require-service-name",
  "type": "validation",
  "from": "source",
  "spec": {
    "driver": "cel",
    "on_mismatch": "reject",
    "cel": {
      "logs": "logs.resource_logs.all(r, r.resource.attributes.exists(a, a.key == 'service.name'))"
    }
  }
}

Additional Examples:

Drop metric deliveries that contain a metric without a name: 

{
  "driver": "cel",
  "on_mismatch": "drop",
  "cel": {
    "metrics": "metrics.resource_metrics.all(r, r.scope_metrics.all(s, s.metrics.all(m, m.name != '')))"
  }
}

Reject trace deliveries that contain a span without a valid trace ID: 

{
  "driver": "cel",
  "on_mismatch": "reject",
  "cel": {
    "traces": "traces.resource_spans.all(r, r.scope_spans.all(s, s.spans.all(span, size(span.trace_id) == 16)))"
  }
}

Reject log deliveries that contain a record whose tenant.id is not a lowercase UUID. matches takes an RE2 regular expression and finds it anywhere in the value, so anchor it with ^ and $. Checking a value that a Broker Sink puts into its NATS subjects keeps out dots, whitespace and wildcards, which would make the subject invalid or change its meaning: 

{
  "driver": "cel",
  "on_mismatch": "reject",
  "cel": {
    "logs": "logs.resource_logs.all(r, r.scope_logs.all(s, s.log_records.all(record, record.attributes.exists(a, a.key == 'tenant.id' && a.value.string_value.matches('^[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}$')))))"
  }
}

Behavior
  • The decision applies to the whole event. An expression like log_records.exists(record, record.severity_text == 'ERROR') passes on a delivery with one ERROR and many INFO records in full, including the INFO records
  • A rule that fails for an event, e.g. a CEL expression accessing a missing list index, rejects the whole event regardless of on_mismatch. The OTLP source answers with HTTP 422, the Broker Source rejects the message instead of redelivering it
  • Place validation stages with on_mismatch: reject before a batch stage, so one invalid delivery does not reject the deliveries batched with it

items.title: Batch Stage
items.text:
Merges events that arrive concurrently into one event, so downstream components handle fewer, larger batches. It batches whatever it receives; use a filter stage before it to batch only some of the data.

Type: batch

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description max_records int No 8192 Flushes once the batch holds at least this many records (log records, metric data points and spans). Events are never split, so a batch can exceed it by the size of the last event max_bytes int No - Flushes a batch before the next event would take it over this many bytes of encoded OTLP data. Without it, the size is not limited timeout string No "200ms" Flushes a batch this long after its first event arrived

Example:

{
  "name": "batch",
  "type": "batch",
  "from": "otlp-in",
  "spec": {
    "max_records": 1000,
    "timeout": "500ms"
  }
}
Behavior
  • Batching happens in memory only. Each caller waits until its batch has been delivered and receives the delivery result, so sources keep acknowledging or rejecting exactly what was delivered, and a slow downstream slows the sources down instead of growing the buffer
  • Batching only helps when events arrive concurrently, e.g. parallel OTLP requests or a Broker Source with several workers. A source that sends one event at a time only adds timeout to its latency
  • Behind an OTLP source, timeout has to stay below the source's delivery_timeout (8s by default), together with the other batch and delay stages on the way to a sink; otherwise the stream is rejected, see Hold Times
  • If a caller's context is cancelled (e.g. the OTLP client disconnects or the OTLP source's delivery_timeout expires) before the batch flushes, its event is withdrawn and not delivered. Once the flush has started, the event is delivered and the caller waits for the result
  • A delivery error, including a rejection by a later stage, applies to every event in the batch. Place validation stages with on_mismatch: reject before the batch, so one invalid event does not reject the others
  • max_bytes keeps batches below a limit downstream, e.g. the NATS server's max_payload (1 MB by default) or the request size a destination accepts. It counts the protobuf encoding of the data, which is what the NATS and OTLP sinks send uncompressed. An event that is larger by itself is sent alone, since events are never split, so the limit downstream can still be exceeded by single large requests. Measuring costs a pass over every event, so it is only done with max_bytes set
  • Events are merged by concatenating their resource entries. Resources and scopes that appear in several events are kept as separate entries, which OTLP allows
  • On shutdown, the open batch is delivered before downstream stages and sinks stop

items.title: Delay Stage
items.text:
Holds every event back for a fixed duration; the caller waits meanwhile, concurrent events in parallel. Useful for testing and simulating slow downstream systems.

Type: delay

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description delay string Yes - Duration to hold each event back (e.g., "100ms", "1s", "5m")

Example:

{
  "name": "delay-stage",
  "type": "delay",
  "from": "source",
  "spec": {
    "delay": "1s"
  }
}
Behavior
  • Behind an OTLP source, the delay counts toward the source's delivery_timeout (8s by default). A stream in which the delay and batch stages on the way to a sink add up to the delivery_timeout or more is rejected, see Hold Times. Raise the delivery_timeout for longer delays

items.title: Encryption Stage
items.text:
Encrypts the body of every log record and the record attributes listed in attributes, so sinks send them encrypted. Attributes it does not list — e.g. the ones a sink's destination expression routes by — stay in cleartext, as do metrics and traces. The key comes from a driver: local (a raw AES-256 key, in a Kubernetes Stream resource via secretKeyRef) or stackit-kms (envelope encryption against the STACKIT KMS, which wraps a per-stage data key once).

Type: encryption

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description driver string Yes - Key source: local or stackit-kms; its options go under a key of the same name algorithm string No aes-256-gcm Payload encryption algorithm attributes []string No - Record attributes to encrypt besides the body (string values only) marker_prefix string No tram.encryption Prefix of the marker attributes set on every encrypted record (<prefix>.algorithm, <prefix>.key_id, <prefix>.wrapped_key); set a neutral prefix if the attribute names should not reveal the product local.key string With driver: local - Base64-encoded 32-byte key; exactly one of key, key_env, key_file local.key_env string With driver: local - Environment variable holding the base64-encoded key local.key_file string With driver: local - File holding the base64-encoded key stackit-kms.project_id string With driver: stackit-kms - STACKIT project UUID stackit-kms.region string With driver: stackit-kms - Region of the key ring, e.g. eu01 stackit-kms.keyring_id string With driver: stackit-kms - Key ring UUID stackit-kms.key_id string With driver: stackit-kms - Key UUID stackit-kms.key_version int With driver: stackit-kms - Version of the key that wraps the data key stackit-kms.endpoint string With driver: stackit-kms https://kms.api.<region>.stackit.cloud KMS API base URL stackit-kms.token string With driver: stackit-kms SDK default auth Bearer token of a STACKIT service account

Example:

{
  "name": "encrypt",
  "type": "encryption",
  "from": "otlp",
  "spec": {
    "driver": "local",
    "local": { "key": "<base64-encoded 32-byte key>" },
    "attributes": ["user.email"]
  }
}

In a Kubernetes Stream resource, the key can come from a secret instead of the spec:

spec:
  stages:
    - name: encrypt
      type: encryption
      from: otlp
      spec:
        driver: local
        local:
          key:
            secretKeyRef: { name: tram-encryption-key, key: key }
        attributes: ["user.email"]

With the stackit-kms driver, the stage generates a random data key once, wraps it via the KMS, and encrypts every record locally with AES-256-GCM:

{
  "name": "encrypt",
  "type": "encryption",
  "from": "otlp",
  "spec": {
    "driver": "stackit-kms",
    "stackit-kms": {
      "project_id": "<project UUID>",
      "region": "eu01",
      "keyring_id": "<key ring UUID>",
      "key_id": "<key UUID>",
      "key_version": 1,
      "token": "<STACKIT service account token>"
    },
    "attributes": ["user.email"]
  }
}

In a Kubernetes Stream resource, the token can come from a secret instead of the spec:

spec:
  stages:
    - name: encrypt
      type: encryption
      from: otlp
      spec:
        driver: stackit-kms
        stackit-kms:
          project_id: <project UUID>
          region: eu01
          keyring_id: <key ring UUID>
          key_id: <key UUID>
          key_version: 1
          token:
            secretKeyRef: { name: stackit-kms-token, key: token }
        attributes: ["user.email"]
Behavior
  • Every encrypted record carries the marker attributes <marker_prefix>.algorithm, <marker_prefix>.key_id and, for KMS drivers, <marker_prefix>.wrapped_key (base64) — by default tram.encryption.*; set marker_prefix to rename them. They are cleartext, so consumers know how to decrypt: with local, the same key; with stackit-kms, KMS Decrypt on the wrapped data key, then local AES-256-GCM. The ciphertext is nonce + AES-256-GCM tag appended, base64-encoded in string fields
  • Routing is unaffected as long as routing attributes are not listed in attributes: the broker and OTLP sinks evaluate their destination expressions on the encrypted event, and cleartext attributes resolve to the same subjects and URLs as without the stage. A listed attribute with a non-string value, or a body that is neither string nor bytes, rejects the event (the OTLP source answers with 422)
  • The stage never modifies the incoming event; it forwards a copy, so sibling branches see the plaintext
  • The stage holds no events back and does not count toward the Hold Times
  • Metrics and traces pass through unchanged; only logs are encrypted

items.title: Decryption Stage
items.text:
Decrypts the body of every encrypted log record and the record attributes listed in attributes, and removes the encryption marker attributes the Encryption Stage sets. Records without a marker attribute pass through unchanged, so the stage is idempotent and can sit in a branch that also receives plaintext. Metrics and traces pass through unchanged. The driver and key have to match the records' tram.encryption.key_id marker, no matter which stream or producer encrypted them: local (the raw AES-256 key, in a Kubernetes Stream resource via secretKeyRef) or stackit-kms (the STACKIT KMS key that wrapped the per-record data key, which the stage unwraps).

Type: decryption

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description driver string Yes - Key source: local or stackit-kms; its options go under a key of the same name algorithm string No aes-256-gcm Payload encryption algorithm of the records; must match the records' tram.encryption.algorithm attributes []string No - Record attributes to decrypt besides the body; list the same ones the encryption stage encrypted marker_prefix string No tram.encryption Prefix of the marker attributes on encrypted records; has to match the prefix the records were encrypted with local.key string With driver: local - Base64-encoded 32-byte key; exactly one of key, key_env, key_file local.key_env string With driver: local - Environment variable holding the base64-encoded key local.key_file string With driver: local - File holding the base64-encoded key stackit-kms.project_id string With driver: stackit-kms - STACKIT project UUID stackit-kms.region string With driver: stackit-kms - Region of the key ring, e.g. eu01 stackit-kms.keyring_id string With driver: stackit-kms - Key ring UUID stackit-kms.key_id string With driver: stackit-kms - Key UUID stackit-kms.key_version int With driver: stackit-kms - Version of the key that unwraps the data key stackit-kms.endpoint string With driver: stackit-kms https://kms.api.<region>.stackit.cloud KMS API base URL stackit-kms.token string With driver: stackit-kms SDK default auth Bearer token of a STACKIT service account

Example:

{
  "name": "decrypt",
  "type": "decryption",
  "from": "encrypt",
  "spec": {
    "driver": "local",
    "local": { "key": "<base64-encoded 32-byte key>" },
    "attributes": ["user.email"]
  }
}

In a Kubernetes Stream resource, the key can come from a secret instead of the spec:

spec:
  stages:
    - name: decrypt
      type: decryption
      from: encrypt
      spec:
        driver: local
        local:
          key:
            secretKeyRef: { name: tram-encryption-key, key: key }
        attributes: ["user.email"]

With the stackit-kms driver, the stage unwraps the wrapped data key of each record via the KMS (cached in memory) and decrypts locally. Point it at the KMS key named in the records' tram.encryption.key_id marker — the encrypted records may well come from a different stream:

{
  "name": "decrypt",
  "type": "decryption",
  "from": "encrypt",
  "spec": {
    "driver": "stackit-kms",
    "stackit-kms": {
      "project_id": "<project UUID>",
      "region": "eu01",
      "keyring_id": "<key ring UUID>",
      "key_id": "<key UUID>",
      "key_version": 1,
      "token": "<STACKIT service account token>"
    },
    "attributes": ["user.email"]
  }
}

In a Kubernetes Stream resource, the token can come from a secret instead of the spec:

spec:
  stages:
    - name: decrypt
      type: decryption
      from: encrypt
      spec:
        driver: stackit-kms
        stackit-kms:
          project_id: <project UUID>
          region: eu01
          keyring_id: <key ring UUID>
          key_id: <key UUID>
          key_version: 1
          token:
            secretKeyRef: { name: stackit-kms-token, key: token }
        attributes: ["user.email"]
Behavior
  • A record is recognized as encrypted by its <marker_prefix>.algorithm attribute (default tram.encryption.algorithm). After decryption the stage removes the marker attributes <marker_prefix>.algorithm, <marker_prefix>.key_id and <marker_prefix>.wrapped_key, so downstream stages and sinks see plaintext again and routing on decrypted attributes works
  • Records without the marker attribute pass through unchanged, as do metrics and traces; only logs are decrypted
  • A record whose tram.encryption.algorithm differs from the stage's algorithm, or whose tram.encryption.key_id differs from the driver's key (e.g. after a key rotation), rejects the event (the OTLP source answers with 422). A listed attribute with a non-string value, or a body that is neither string nor bytes, rejects the event as well
  • With stackit-kms, the wrapped data key of each record is unwrapped via KMS Decrypt and cached in memory, so repeated records do not call the KMS again
  • The stage never modifies the incoming event; it forwards a copy, so sibling branches see the ciphertext
  • The stage holds no events back and does not count toward the Hold Times

items.title: No-op Stage
items.text:
A pass-through stage that performs no processing — for testing, debugging, or as a placeholder.

Type: noop

Configuration: None required.

Example:

{
  "name": "passthrough",
  "type": "noop",
  "from": "source"
}

items.title: Value Map Stage
items.text:
Looks up a source attribute in a table for every record and sets a target attribute to the mapped value, or to default on a miss (missing attribute or no table entry). Every record is passed on; nothing is filtered, dropped or held back.

Type: value_map

Configuration:

Field Type Required Default Description source_attr string Yes - Attribute whose value is looked up target_attr string Yes - Attribute set to the result of the lookup. An existing attribute of that name is replaced default string Yes - Value set when the source attribute is missing or its value has no table entry level string No "record" Level the source attribute is read from: record (the record's own attributes) or resource (the attributes of the record's resource) table object One of table, table_ref - Embedded lookup table, source value to target value. In a Kubernetes Stream resource, the table can come from config maps selected by label, which keeps large tables out of the resource; see Config Maps table_ref string One of table, table_ref - Path to a JSON file that holds the lookup table as an object of string values, e.g. {"value-a": "target-a"}. Read once when the stage is created; an unreadable file or invalid JSON is rejected. Exactly one of table and table_ref has to be set

The target attribute is always set on the record itself, whatever level the source attribute is read from. A source value that is not a string cannot have a table entry and receives the default value.

Example: translate a team attribute into a team.id attribute:

{
  "name": "team-ids",
  "type": "value_map",
  "from": "otlp-in",
  "spec": {
    "source_attr": "team",
    "target_attr": "team.id",
    "default": "unassigned",
    "table": {
      "team-0": "cart",
      "team-1": "checkout"
    }
  }
}

Metrics: besides the node metrics of its stream, the stage records its lookup outcomes, with the stream, the node of the stage and the signal as labels:

Metric Type Labels Description tram_stage_value_map_mapped_total Counter stream, node, signal Records whose source value the table maps, which received the mapped value tram_stage_value_map_lookup_missing_attr_total Counter stream, node, signal Records without the source attribute, which received the default value tram_stage_value_map_lookup_no_entry_total Counter stream, node, signal Records whose source value has no table entry, which received the default value

The node metrics framework counts records and durations only, not lookup outcomes, which is why the stage adds its own counters, created from the meter provider its factory passes. They are labeled like the node metrics, so every stream and stage has a series of its own.

Behavior
  • A lookup miss is a defined state, not an error: the record is still passed on, with the target attribute set to default
  • Every record is annotated, so the stage always passes on a copy of the event: the containers it annotates (records of each signal) are rebuilt, resources, scopes and metric metadata are shared
  • The table is fixed while the stream runs. To change it, update the stream with a changed spec, through the API, the config sync or a Stream resource, or change the config maps a Stream resource selects its table from; the usual stream update applies: an update with an identical spec changes nothing, an update with just a changed spec replaces the stage without touching the source
  • The stage holds no events back and does not count toward the Hold Times

items.title: API Endpoints
items.text:
The TRAM service provides the following HTTP endpoints:

Method Endpoint Description GET /v1/streams List all streams, ordered by name PUT /v1/streams/{name} Create or update a stream GET /v1/streams/{name} Get a stream configuration DELETE /v1/streams/{name} Delete a stream GET /metrics Metrics of TRAM in the Prometheus format, see Metrics

The stream name is taken from the URL; a name in the request body is replaced by it.

items.title: Create a Pipeline with Stages
items.text:
This example adds a noop stage between the source and sinks:

curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/processing-pipeline \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "stream": {
      "name": "processing-pipeline",
      "source": {
        "name": "events-source",
        "type": "generator",
        "spec": {
          "interval": "1s"
        }
      },
      "stages": [
        {
          "name": "passthrough",
          "type": "noop",
          "from": "events-source"
        }
      ],
      "sinks": [
        {
          "name": "console",
          "type": "debug",
          "from": "passthrough"
        }
      ]
    }
  }'

items.title: Get Stream Configuration
items.text: curl http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/my-pipeline

items.title: Delete a Stream
items.text: curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/my-pipeline

items.title: Configuration Sources
items.text: Besides the API, streams can be managed from two further sources. All of them change the same set of streams.

items.title: File Sync
items.text:
./tram server --enable-file-sync --config-dir config

Every <name>.json file in the directory describes one stream, in the same format as the API request body ({"stream": {...}}); see examples/config/ for examples. The file name, without .json, is the stream name. The sync works in both directions:

  • Adding, changing or deleting a file creates, updates or deletes the stream
  • Streams created or changed through the API or the Kubernetes operator are written to files (new files are readable only by the owner, mode 0600), and deleted streams have their file removed
  • Streams without a file are deleted when the directory is synced
  • A stream that cannot be created or updated, e.g. because NATS is not reachable yet when TRAM starts, is tried again without its file changing: after 1 second, then with a delay that doubles up to 30 seconds, until every stream is applied. Changing a file starts over with the shortest delay. A stream that keeps failing is logged once a minute; one that is applied after failing is logged once more. A file that is invalid for good is tried again as well, so fix or remove it

items.title: Kubernetes Operator
items.text:
kubectl apply -f manifests/crds/io.tram.core_streams.yaml
./tram server --enable-k8s-operator

The operator watches Stream resources (io.tram.core/v1) and runs each as a stream named <namespace>.<name>. It uses the in-cluster configuration or the current kubeconfig context; --kubeconfig selects another file. By default every TRAM instance runs every Stream resource in the cluster, including those that name engines. With --watch-namespace limits an instance to some namespaces, and --engine to the Stream resources of one Engine. See the operator documentation for details.

Alternatively, tram manager runs Engine resources (io.tram.core/v1alpha1) as Deployments of TRAM instances, and a Stream names the engines that run it in spec.engineRefs; see Engines and examples/k8s/. The Helm chart charts/tram, or the kustomization in manifests/, installs the manager with the CRDs:

helm install tram oci://ghcr.io/go-tram/charts/tram --version 0.0.20 --namespace tram-system --create-namespace
# or
kubectl apply --server-side -f https://github.com/GO-TRAM/TRAM/releases/download/v0.0.20/tram.yaml

Every release publishes the chart and the manifests with its version; from the repository, charts/tram and kubectl apply --server-side -k manifests/ deploy the image latest.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
git clone https://github.com/GO-TRAM/TRAM.git tram
cd tram
go build -o tram ./cmd/tram

Or build a container image with Docker or Podman: task image:build (with Task) or docker build -t tram:dev .. Run task to see all development tasks, e.g. for tests and benchmarks; CONTRIBUTING.md explains them.

items.title: Run
items.text:
./tram server

The container image starts the server with both APIs listening on all interfaces of the container: docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -p 50051:50051 tram:dev.

By default the HTTP API listens on localhost:8080 and the gRPC API on localhost:50051. --log-level sets the log level (debug, info, warn or error; default info). See ./tram server --help for all flags.

items.title: Create a First Stream
items.text:
Create a stream whose generator source emits an event every 5 seconds and whose debug sink logs it to stdout:

curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/my-pipeline \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "stream": {
      "name": "my-pipeline",
      "source": {
        "name": "event-generator",
        "type": "generator",
        "spec": {
          "interval": "5s"
        }
      },
      "sinks": [
        {
          "name": "console",
          "type": "debug",
          "from": "event-generator"
        }
      ]
    }
  }'

More examples are under Example API Usage.

items.title: Metrics
items.text:
GET /metrics on the HTTP API serves TRAM's metrics in the Prometheus format, for Prometheus or any other scraper. By default the source and the sinks of every stream are measured, whatever their type, and the stages are not; see Choosing the metrics of a stream:

Metric Type Labels Description tram_node_records_total Counter stream, node, kind, signal Records the node received: log records, metric data points and spans. kind is source, stage or sink, signal is logs, metrics or traces tram_node_records_out_total Counter stream, node, kind, signal Records a source or stage passed on: log records, metric data points and spans. With several children, each record counts once, not once per child. Sinks pass nothing on tram_node_duration_seconds Histogram stream, node, kind, outcome Time the node took to handle an event. outcome is ok, rejected (the event was refused for good, e.g. by a validation stage), cancelled (the caller gave up, e.g. an OTLP client that closed its connection) or error. An expired delivery_timeout counts as error, since then TRAM took too long tram_source_request_size_bytes Histogram stream, node, kind, encoding, body Size of the requests a source decoded events from, such as the OTLP source. body is received (as sent, e.g. gzip-compressed) or decoded (after undoing the content encoding), encoding is gzip or identity. Sources that consume messages, like the broker source, report nothing

The endpoint also serves the Go runtime (go_*) and process (process_*) metrics.

For a source, the records are what it accepted and passed on, each counted once however many branches the stream has, and the outcome is the result its client gets: an event a single branch fails fails for the client. Events a source refuses before passing them on, such as an OTLP request that cannot be decoded, are not counted.

Events pass through a stream synchronously, so the duration of a source or stage includes the stages and sinks below it, and for a batch stage the time an event waits for its batch to be flushed. The duration of a source is the time its client waits for TRAM. Only the duration of a sink is its own.

So the time a stream's stages take, including the wait of a batch stage, is the duration of its source minus that of its sinks, without measuring the stages themselves.

A stage's input minus its output is what it dropped, so the share each stage drops, for streams that measure the records of their stages, is:

1 - sum by (stream, node) (rate(tram_node_records_out_total{kind="stage"}[5m]))
  / sum by (stream, node) (rate(tram_node_records_total{kind="stage"}[5m]))

The average size of the requests a source received, compressed as sent and decoded, and the share of requests above 1 MB, half of a common 2 MB ingress limit:

sum by (stream, body) (rate(tram_source_request_size_bytes_sum[5m]))
  / sum by (stream, body) (rate(tram_source_request_size_bytes_count[5m]))

1 - sum by (stream) (rate(tram_source_request_size_bytes_bucket{body="received",le="1.048576e+06"}[5m]))
  / sum by (stream) (rate(tram_source_request_size_bytes_count{body="received"}[5m]))

A stage that drops every record of a signal, such as a filter whose CEL expression for it is "false", has no output series for that signal, so drop the signal label or use or vector(0) when comparing per signal.

items.title: Choosing the metrics of a stream
items.text:
Every node is a series of its own per metric, so many streams with several stages each add up to many series. The optional metrics field of a stream turns each metric on or off per kind of node; fields left out keep their defaults:

Field Metrics Defaults records tram_node_records_total and tram_node_records_out_total source: true, stages: false, sinks: true duration tram_node_duration_seconds source: true, stages: false, sinks: true request_size tram_source_request_size_bytes true

To see what each stage of a stream drops and how long it takes:

"metrics": {
  "records": {"stages": true},
  "duration": {"stages": true}
}

The field is part of the stream in the API, in the files of the file sync and in the Stream resource of the Kubernetes operator (spec.metrics). Changing it rewires the stream's stages and sinks but keeps its source running. Series of a node that stops being measured stay at their last value until TRAM restarts.

items.title: Security
items.text:
TRAM has no authentication or authorization of its own. Whoever can create a stream decides which ports TRAM opens and where it sends data, so treat access to every configuration source like access to the TRAM process:

  • API: the gRPC and HTTP APIs accept every request. They listen on localhost by default; if you bind them to other interfaces with --grpc-endpoint and --http-endpoint, restrict access, e.g. with a network policy or an authenticating proxy in front
  • Profiling: --pprof-endpoint serves the Go profiles under /debug/pprof/ on their own endpoint, without authentication; it is off by default. Profiles reveal internals such as stack traces and command-line arguments, so bind it to localhost or a port that is not exposed, and reach it with kubectl port-forward. It also turns on mutex and block profiling, which costs a little on contended locks
  • OTLP source: listens on the configured port on all network interfaces, without TLS or authentication. Anyone who can reach the port can send data into the stream. Restrict it on the network level, or terminate TLS and authenticate in a proxy in front of it
  • Sinks: an OTLP sink sends data to any URL in its spec, and insecure: true turns off certificate checks. Keep credentials in sink specs, e.g. in headers or NATS URLs, out of version control; the file sync writes new files readable only by their owner
  • Kubernetes operator: watches Stream resources in all namespaces unless --watch-namespace is set, so everyone allowed to create a Stream in a watched namespace can open ports on the TRAM pod and send data anywhere TRAM can reach. A Stream can also refer to secrets and config maps in its namespace, which TRAM reads and passes to the stream, so its author can send their values anywhere. Grant create on streams.io.tram.core only to users you would also trust with the TRAM deployment and with the secrets and config maps of that namespace. spec.engineRefs is no access control either: anyone who can create a Stream in an Engine's namespace can run it on that Engine

items.title: Pipeline Structure
items.text:
Streams follow a tree structure with these rules:

  1. Each pipeline has exactly one source (root)
  2. Stages can be connected to the source or other stages
  3. Sinks must be connected to either the source or a stage
  4. All leaves must be sinks (no dangling stages)
flowchart LR
    subgraph stream["Stream"]
        source(["Source"]) --> stage["Stage"]
        stage --> sink(["Sink"])
        source --> sink
        stage --> stage
    end

items.title: Data Flow
items.text:
Source → [Stage] → Sink

Arrows represent the direction of data flow, from source to sinks.

Type Components Sources broker, generator, otlp Stages batch, delay, filter, noop, validation, value_map Sinks broker, debug, otlp

For detailed documentation on each component and its configuration, see COMPONENTS.md.

    broker_src(["broker source"]) --> tram

items.title: Fan-out Pattern
items.text:
Route data from a single source to multiple sinks. Every sink receives every event:

curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/fanout-example \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data-binary @- <<'EOF'
{
  "stream": {
    "name": "fanout-example",
    "source": {
      "name": "otlp-in",
      "type": "otlp",
      "spec": { "http_port": 4318 }
    },
    "sinks": [
      {
        "name": "console",
        "type": "debug",
        "from": "otlp-in"
      },
      {
        "name": "archive",
        "type": "broker",
        "from": "otlp-in",
        "spec": {
          "driver": "nats",
          "nats": { "url": "nats://localhost:4222" },
          "destination": {
            "logs": "'logs.' + logs.resource_logs[0].resource.attributes.get_attr('service.name')"
          }
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}
EOF

The broker sink with driver: nats needs a NATS server with JetStream enabled, e.g. docker compose -f examples/nats/docker-compose.yaml up -d, and a stream for its subjects, which TRAM does not create: nats stream add telemetry --subjects 'logs.>' --defaults.

items.title: Chained Stages
items.text:
Process data through multiple stages before reaching sinks:

curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/v1/streams/chained-pipeline \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "stream": {
      "name": "chained-pipeline",
      "source": {
        "name": "source",
        "type": "generator",
        "spec": { "interval": "1s" }
      },
      "stages": [
        {
          "name": "stage1",
          "type": "noop",
          "from": "source"
        },
        {
          "name": "stage2",
          "type": "noop",
          "from": "stage1"
        }
      ],
      "sinks": [
        {
          "name": "output",
          "type": "debug",
          "from": "stage2"
        }
      ]
    }
  }'

items.title: Updating a Stream
items.text:
A PUT to an existing stream changes as little as possible:

Change Effect None Nothing happens; the running stream is kept Stages, sinks or metrics only The new stages and sinks are created, events still in flight finish in the old ones, and the source switches over. The source keeps running, e.g. an OTLP source keeps its port open, and no event is lost Source The stream is stopped and created again. An OTLP source closes its port in between, so clients briefly cannot connect

If an update fails, e.g. because of an invalid component spec, the request returns an error and the previous version of the stream keeps running. Delete and create a stream to restart it completely.

items.title: Dry Run
items.text:
PUT /v1/streams/{name} with "dry_run": true in the request body validates the stream and reports what applying it would do, without changing the running stream. The flag is a field of the request body, not a query parameter, because the PUT body maps to the whole request message. The response holds a plan:

{
  "stream": { "...": "the requested stream" },
  "plan": {
    "action": "STREAM_PLAN_ACTION_HOT_SWAP",
    "sourceReplaced": false,
    "createdNodes": ["enrich"],
    "stoppedNodes": ["old-sink"]
  }
}

action is STREAM_PLAN_ACTION_NOOP (nothing would change), STREAM_PLAN_ACTION_HOT_SWAP (the source keeps running and its stages and sinks are replaced below it) or STREAM_PLAN_ACTION_REBUILD (the stream is new, stopped, or its source changed: it would be stopped and created again). An invalid spec is rejected with 400 as usual; nothing is applied either way.

If the source of a stream stops on its own, e.g. because the NATS stream of a broker source does not exist yet, TRAM restarts the stream after a delay that grows from 1 second to 1 minute while it keeps failing. A PUT of the unchanged stream restarts it right away.

items.title: Testing a Stream
items.text:
A stream can carry test cases in tests. They are never run by loading the stream; only an explicit test run executes them:

tram test stream.json [--secrets secrets.json]

The file holds either a bare stream object or a file sync file that wraps it in {"stream": {...}}, like the examples in examples/tests/; see examples/tests/otlp_with_filters.json for a stream with test cases.

The stream is loaded into its own in-memory tree: the source is replaced by a test source that emits the test inputs, and every sink by a capture sink, so no external system is contacted. The stages are the real stages and process the events.

Each test has a name, an input event and the expected outcome per sink in expect:

  • "out": <event> — sink out must receive exactly this event. Events are OTLP JSON objects with one of the keys logs, metrics or traces
  • "out": "drop" — sink out must receive nothing
  • "out": "reject" — the event must be rejected by a stage
  • a sink without an entry in expect must receive nothing
"tests": [
  {
    "name": "keeps real logs",
    "input":  {"logs": {"resourceLogs": [{"scopeLogs": [{"logRecords": [{"body": {"stringValue": "hello"}}]}]}]}},
    "expect": {"out": {"logs": {"resourceLogs": [{"scopeLogs": [{"logRecords": [{"body": {"stringValue": "hello"}}]}]}]}}}
  },
  {
    "name": "drops noise",
    "input":  {"logs": {"resourceLogs": [{"scopeLogs": [{"logRecords": [{"body": {"stringValue": "noise"}}]}]}]}},
    "expect": {"out": "drop"}
  }
]

--secrets reads a JSON file mapping "<name>/<key>" to values and resolves secretKeyRef references in stage specs. A reference that cannot be resolved is an error naming the reference, never its value. Source and sink specs are not used by a test run. The exit code is 0 when all tests pass and 1 otherwise.
